client: I've been really struggling lately with my new job at this tech startup. The hours are insane — I've been staying late almost every night for the past month, and I feel like I'm constantly drowning in tasks that never seem to end. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the work is still going to be there tomorrow no matter what.
therapist: What you're carrying sounds genuinely exhausting — and I notice that even as you're describing all of this, there's a quiet heaviness in your voice, like you're worn down beneath the surface. That thought that talking won't change anything is really worth exploring, because while the workload will still be there tomorrow, how you *relate* to it — the meaning you make of it, the boundaries you feel entitled to set — that *can* shift. You reached out today, and that's actually evidence that some part of you believes change is possible, even when another part feels defeated.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying about relating to it differently, but honestly, I'm not sure how much of this is about my mindset versus just... the actual situation being overwhelming. Like, even if I somehow made peace with the workload in my head, I'd still be at my desk at 9pm every night with more tasks piling up. And the part about setting boundaries — I've thought about that, but I'm terrified that if I push back or leave on time, people will think I'm not committed enough and I'll lose the job before I've even really started.
therapist: You're making a really important and valid point — this isn't *just* a mindset issue, and I don't want to minimize the very real pressure you're under. But I'm also noticing something in how you're speaking — your voice is quiet, almost careful, like you're holding something fragile — and that fear that leaving on time would make you look uncommitted is worth gently examining: is that a fact you *know*, or is it a prediction your anxious mind is making to keep you "safe"? Sometimes when we're new and already overwhelmed, our minds generate worst-case rules that feel like certainties but are actually assumptions worth testing.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess when you put it that way, I can see it might be more of an assumption than a fact — but it doesn't feel like just an assumption, you know? My manager has made a few comments about people who "aren't all in," and a couple of my coworkers are always online late too, so there's this unspoken culture that feels pretty real. It's hard to separate what's actually expected from what I'm just telling myself.
therapist: You're right to hold onto that — this isn't pure imagination, there are real signals in your environment feeding that fear, and it makes complete sense that it's hard to untangle. I notice you sound quite soft and tentative as you say this, like you're carefully weighing each word, which tells me this uncertainty feels genuinely unsettling rather than just a passing worry. A useful next step in CBT would be to separate what your manager has *actually said about you specifically* from the more general cultural signals you're picking up — because right now your mind may be merging those two things into one solid "rule," when they might actually be telling different stories.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That distinction actually makes some sense to me, and I can see how I might be blending those things together. But when I try to think about what my manager has said specifically to me, I realize I don't have a lot of direct feedback either way — which almost makes it worse, because the silence feels like I'm just waiting for something bad to happen. It's like the uncertainty itself is the thing that's eating at me, not even a real criticism.
therapist: That insight is really significant — you've just identified that the enemy right now isn't actual criticism, it's the *not knowing*, and your mind is rushing in to fill that silence with threat. Interestingly, even as you describe feeling eaten up by uncertainty, there's something in your voice that sounds almost energized by this realization, like a part of you is waking up to something important. In CBT, we'd call what you're experiencing "ambiguity intolerance," and one powerful step is to consider whether you could actively *seek* that feedback rather than waiting for it — because getting real information, even if imperfect, almost always feels better than the stories our minds invent in the silence.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Seeking feedback sounds reasonable in theory, but the idea of actually going to my manager and asking how I'm doing makes my stomach drop. What if I open that door and the answer is worse than the silence — like what if asking itself signals that I'm not confident enough, or draws attention to the fact that I'm struggling? I think part of me would rather keep my head down and hope things become clearer on their own, even though I know that's probably not a great strategy.
therapist: I can hear how fast your thoughts are racing right now — there's a real spike of anxiety in your voice, like this possibility genuinely alarmed you — and that makes complete sense, because you're essentially weighing one fear against another. But notice what your mind just did: it took a neutral action, asking for feedback, and rapidly generated two threatening interpretations — that it signals weakness, *and* that it exposes struggle — which is actually your anxious thinking working overtime to protect you from uncertainty by making the "safe" option feel safer. Most managers experience employees who proactively seek feedback as *more* confident and self-aware, not less — so it's worth asking whether "keep your head down and hope" has any real evidence behind it, or whether that's the anxiety talking.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I know you're probably right that keeping my head down isn't really a strategy, it's just avoidance — but even hearing that doesn't make the fear go away. And I think what makes it harder is that I'm already so depleted from the long hours that I don't have much emotional reserve left to take a risk that might backfire. Like, if I asked for feedback and it went badly, I'm not sure I have the bandwidth right now to handle that on top of everything else.
therapist: What you just said deserves to be really heard — you're not just anxious about this, you're running on empty, and there's something in your voice, a kind of stretched thinness, that tells me this depletion is very real and not something to push through or rationalize away. That's actually crucial information, because CBT isn't about forcing brave actions when you're genuinely depleted — it's about finding the *right-sized* step for where you actually are right now. So rather than a full feedback conversation with your manager, could there be a smaller, lower-stakes way to get just a little more information — something that costs you less emotionally but still chips away at that silence?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: A smaller step does feel more manageable than a big formal conversation, and I guess I could maybe just mention something casual in passing, like asking if there's anything specific I should be focusing on this week. But I'm second-guessing even that, because I'm not sure I'd be able to read whether the response was genuinely positive or just polite, and then I'd probably spend the rest of the day overanalyzing every word they said. I think my brain is just so primed to look for danger signals right now that even good information might not actually land as reassuring.
therapist: There's something really telling in what you just described — your words carry a kind of weary resignation, but your voice has a slightly lighter quality to it, like part of you is actually relieved to have found a smaller step that feels doable. You've just identified something really sophisticated about yourself: that right now your threat-detection system is so sensitized that even neutral or positive information gets filtered through a danger lens — and that's not a character flaw, that's what chronic depletion and stress *do* to a brain. So the work right now might be less about gathering the perfect information and more about gently lowering that alarm system first — which means sleep, small moments of recovery, and self-compassion — so that when good information does come, you actually have the capacity to let it land.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: The idea of prioritizing sleep and recovery sounds nice, but it feels almost laughable given that I'm leaving work at 9pm and then lying awake thinking about everything I didn't finish. I want to believe self-compassion is something I can actually access right now, but honestly it feels like a luxury I haven't earned yet — like I need to first get on top of the work before I'm allowed to give myself a break. I know that's probably a trap, but I can't seem to convince myself otherwise.
therapist: The way you just said that — quickly, with a kind of urgent energy in your voice — tells me this belief that you have to *earn* rest is something you feel very strongly, almost like a rule you're defending. But you already named it yourself: it's a trap, and it's a particularly cruel one because it ensures the permission to rest never actually arrives — there will always be more work to justify one more late night first. That belief isn't a truth about how recovery works; it's an exhausted mind trying to maintain control, and gently challenging it might start with one small question: has pushing harder *ever* actually cleared the pile enough to finally feel like you've earned that break?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: When you ask it that way, I have to admit the honest answer is no — the pile has never actually cleared, not once in the past month. But there's this stubborn part of me that keeps thinking this time will be different, like if I just push a little harder this week it'll finally tip into something manageable. I know logically that's not how it's working, but letting go of that belief feels almost dangerous, like if I stop pushing I'll just fall completely behind and everything will fall apart.
therapist: You just gave yourself a really important piece of evidence — one month, not once, and yet that part of you keeps moving the finish line, which tells me this isn't really about the work at all, it's about a deeper fear that if you stop bracing, everything collapses. I notice you said that very quickly and softly, like the words were tumbling out under pressure, which makes me think that "dangerous" feeling is very alive in your body right now, not just a thought. That belief that constant pushing is the only thing holding everything together is worth examining gently — because what if the pushing itself is part of what's making the pile unmanageable, by keeping you too depleted to work with the clarity and focus that would actually help?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: That reframe actually lands differently than I expected — like, I hadn't considered that the exhaustion itself might be making me slower and less effective, which would mean the pushing is kind of self-defeating. But even understanding that intellectually, I don't know how to just... stop the cycle, because every time I try to leave earlier or give myself a break, the guilt hits immediately and it feels unbearable. It's like my brain won't let me rest without punishing me for it.
therapist: The speed and pitch in your voice right now tells me that guilt hits fast and hard — almost like an alarm that fires before you've even had a chance to consciously choose rest. What you're describing is really common in people who've internalized the belief that their worth is tied to their output — the guilt isn't a signal that you're doing something wrong, it's a conditioned response, and like any conditioned response, it can be gradually retrained. One small but powerful place to start is to practice sitting with that guilt for just a few minutes without acting on it — not to make it disappear, but to slowly teach your nervous system that rest won't actually cause the catastrophe it's warning you about.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
